My name is Mark Holland. Two winters ago, I learned the difference between being strong and being saved.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley standing outside a chain-link fence of a closed machine shop, a heavy chain and padlock on the gate, a white paper notice on the fence, gray overcast winter day, light snow
For nineteen years I ran a lathe at the same shop outside Saginaw. I was good at it. I could fix anything.
Then one Friday in November, they chained the gate. No warning. Just a paper on the fence, and a final check.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley and a 38 year old white Caucasian woman with shoulder-length dirty blonde hair, wearing a cream knit cardigan sitting at a small wooden kitchen table at night covered with scattered bills and envelopes, she looks worried, he forces a reassuring look, warm pendant lamp
I told my wife Jenna not to worry. I said it like a man who had a plan.
I didn't have a plan. I had a resume nobody called back, a truck payment, a mortgage, and two kids who still thought their dad could do anything.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley sitting alone at a kitchen table late at night lit by the glow of an old laptop, a stack of printed job applications beside him, coffee mug, exhausted
I did everything you're supposed to do. I applied for forty-one jobs. I drove to job fairs. I sold my tools, one by one.
And every week, the pile on the table got higher. And something inside me got quieter.

a tow truck hooking up a red pickup truck in a snowy driveway on a gray morning, seen through a frosted living room window, a 9 year old white Caucasian girl with long light blonde hair in a single braid wearing a pastel purple sweater standing at the window in socks watching, back view
In February, they came for the truck. Lily, she's nine, stood at the front window in her socks and watched them hook it up.
She didn't cry. She just looked at me. I think that was worse.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley sitting alone on an overturned bucket in a cold dim garage at night, elbows on knees, head down, single bare bulb, empty pegboard where tools used to hang
That's when hopeless turned into helpless.
Hopeless is when you can't see a way out. Helpless is when you stop believing your own hands can make one.
I would sit in the garage after everyone went to bed. Not doing anything. Just sitting. I didn't want anyone to see me like that.

a 38 year old white Caucasian woman with shoulder-length dirty blonde hair, wearing a cream knit cardigan standing in the doorway between the house and a dim garage at night, warm light behind her, reaching out a hand, pleading expression
Mark, talk to me. Call somebody. Call your brother. Call Pastor Dave. Pray with me.
And I said the thing I'm not proud of. I said, Pray? Jenna, prayer doesn't pay the mortgage. I need to do something.
a 14 year old white Caucasian boy with messy brown hair wearing a dark green hoodie sitting on a dark wooden staircase at night, listening, hugging his knees, light from a doorway below
I didn't know Owen was on the stairs. He's fourteen.
He came down the next morning while I was staring at my coffee, and he asked me a question I couldn't answer.

a 14 year old white Caucasian boy with messy brown hair wearing a dark green hoodie sitting across a kitchen table from a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley in morning light, the boy asking an earnest question, the father staring into a coffee mug
He said, Dad, at youth group they keep telling us, when you've got nobody else to call, call on Jesus.
But isn't that just what you say when you've given up? Like, if you can't fix it, you pray?

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley standing in a kitchen holding a smartphone face down in his hand, jaw set, looking out a frosty window, stubborn proud expression
I wanted to tell him yes. That's what I believed. Praying was for when the real work ran out.
Reaching for your phone was for scrolling, not for help. A man doesn't reach out. A man figures it out.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley sitting in a dark garage at three in the morning, his face lit only by the glow of a smartphone in his hands, earbuds in
But that night, at three in the morning, I had nothing left to figure it out with.
Jenna had put an app on my phone weeks before. Community Covenant. I'd never opened it. I told myself I was just going to look. I pressed play.
close-up of a smartphone glowing in a man's rough hands in the dark, a scripture reading playing on the screen, earbuds, soft bokeh, the screen text is blurry and unreadable
I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the Lord, which made heaven and earth. Psalm one twenty one.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley in a dark garage, head bowed, eyes closed, a tear on his cheek, phone held to his chest, faint dawn-blue light from a small window
My help cometh. Not, my help is coming once I've done enough.
And then the reel said something I've never forgotten. When Peter was sinking in the water, he didn't swim first. He didn't come up with a plan.
He cried, saying, Lord, save me. And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him. Matthew fourteen, thirty and thirty one.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley typing slowly on a smartphone with both thumbs in a dim garage, focused, vulnerable, close medium shot
Crying out was not giving up. Crying out was the first thing Peter did right.
So I did the one thing I could do. I opened the box that says, How are you doing? And for the first time in four months, I told the truth.
I typed, I'm not okay. I lost my job. I lost my truck. I don't know who I am if I can't provide. I don't have anybody else to call.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley waking up on an old couch in a garage, early morning golden sunlight streaming through a small window, looking at his smartphone with a surprised softened face
I fell asleep out there. When I woke up, there was a reply waiting. A real one. Somebody had read every word.
Mark, you are not alone, and you were never meant to carry this by yourself. Romans ten thirteen says, whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.
Calling is not the end of your work. It is the beginning of it.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley and a 14 year old white Caucasian boy with messy brown hair wearing a dark green hoodie sitting side by side at a kitchen table with an open Bible between them, morning light, the father explaining, the son listening closely
That's what I finally got to tell Owen. Son, calling on Jesus isn't what you do instead of doing something. It's the first something.
Faith comes first. The Bible says, without faith it is impossible to please him. Hebrews eleven, six.
Noah didn't build the ark and then believe. He believed God. And then he picked up the hammer.
close-up of a man's weathered hands picking up an old wooden-handled hammer from a workbench, sawdust, warm workshop light, shallow depth of field
And faith that never picks up the hammer isn't really faith. James says it plain.
Faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone. James two, seventeen.
So the order matters. Faith first, then the work. The root, then the fruit.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley and a 38 year old white Caucasian woman with shoulder-length dirty blonde hair, wearing a cream knit cardigan at a kitchen table in morning light with their hands resting together on a stack of printed job applications, eyes closed, praying quietly
So every morning after that, before I opened the laptop, Jenna and I put our hands on the stack of applications and prayed Proverbs sixteen, three.
Commit thy works unto the Lord, and thy thoughts shall be established.
I'd been trying to establish my own thoughts for months. They kept falling apart. So I started committing the work first.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley wearing a red work apron with a name tag, stocking shelves in a small-town hardware store aisle, humble but steady expression
Nothing changed overnight. I'm not going to tell you a check showed up in the mailbox. What changed was me.
I took a part-time job at the hardware store in town. Eleven dollars an hour. The old me would have been too proud.
The new me said, Lord, establish the work of my hands. Even this work. Psalm ninety, seventeen.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley and a 14 year old white Caucasian boy with messy brown hair wearing a dark green hoodie rebuilding a wooden front porch together on a sunny cold Saturday, father showing son how to use a drill, snow melting on the lawn
I started fixing things again. A widow down the road had a furnace that wouldn't light. I fixed it for free.
A man at church needed his porch rebuilt. Owen and I did it together, on Saturdays.
I wasn't waiting for God to move anymore. I was moving with Him.

And I kept writing in the app. Some days it was just gratitude. Some days it was, still nothing. And somebody always wrote back.
One morning, a member I had never met read my log, and wrote that her brother-in-law ran a plant two hours south. They were hiring machinists.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley wearing safety glasses operating a metal lathe in a bright clean modern machine shop, confident, sparks of light, focused and at peace
I start every shift there now. It took nine months from the day they chained the gate. Nine months of faith and works, walking side by side.
Two are better than one, the Bible says. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow. Ecclesiastes four.

a white Caucasian family of four laughing together around a dinner table in a warm cozy kitchen at evening, a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley, a 38 year old white Caucasian woman with shoulder-length dirty blonde hair, wearing a cream knit cardigan, a 14 year old white Caucasian boy with messy brown hair wearing a dark green hoodie, a 9 year old white Caucasian girl with long light blonde hair in a single braid wearing a pastel purple sweater, candle light, simple home-cooked meal
So why do we tell you to call on Jesus when you have nobody else to call? Because when you have nobody else, He is still there.
And because calling is not quitting. Reaching for your phone at three in the morning to say, I'm not okay. That's not weakness.
That's the bravest work there is. It's the first work. Everything else gets built on top of it.

a 40 year old white Caucasian man with short light brown hair and a short brown beard, tired eyes, wearing a faded navy canvas work jacket over a gray henley kneeling and hugging a 9 year old white Caucasian girl with long light blonde hair in a single braid wearing a pastel purple sweater by a living room window with gentle snow falling outside, warm lamp light, tender moment
Lily asked me last week if I was scared back then. I told her the truth. Yes.
But scared and alone are two different things. I was scared. I was never alone. And neither are you.
sunrise over a snowy Michigan field with a long country road and a single wooden fence, golden light breaking through clouds, hopeful, no people
If you're in your own winter right now, don't wait until you've fixed it to reach out. Call on Him first. Then pick up the hammer.
Community Covenant. Press play. Tell the truth. Somebody will write back.
